content: National HIS standards and tools are available to guide the development of appropriate policies, guidelines, strategic plans, and roadmaps, including system interoperability. Routine programmatic data collection typically captures information on individuals who access health services at facilities or through community outreach. However, to gain a comprehensive understanding that includes individuals not reached by these services, routine data must be supplemented with data from population-based surveys (e.g., Demographic and Health Surveys or bio-behavioral surveys), modeling tools (e.g., Spectrum AIDS Impact Module), and special studies. These additional data sources help validate and triangulate assessments of program performance and impact. Many health services are delivered in community settings to improve accessibility for individuals who may prefer these over traditional health facilities. Data systems should enable standardized, bidirectional data flow between community-based services and health facilities to enhance program monitoring and data utilization. With the increasing adoption of differentiated care models, HIV prevention, testing, and treatment services are being integrated at the community level, with strong links to facility-based services and data systems. Community engagement, particularly through community-led monitoring, plays a critical role in improving the quality of HIV services. This approach empowers communities to monitor access to and quality of health services, fostering accountability and driving improvements. The 2021 WHO Consolidated Guidelines on HIV Prevention, Testing, Treatment, Service Delivery, and Monitoring emphasize the importance of community-led monitoring in enhancing service quality for people living with HIV. Structured input from community-led monitoring is a vital component of national HIV health information systems, functioning independently from routine clinical data systems. This mechanism empowers communities to influence decision-making processes and improve service delivery. The 2022 WHO Consolidated Guidelines on Person-Centered HIV Strategic Information aim to consolidate recommended data elements, indicators, and guidance on data systems and usage across the spectrum of HIV services. These guidelines emphasize the principle of collect data once, use it many times, promoting efficiency and effectiveness in health information systems. They introduce a minimum dataset for HIV prevention, testing, treatment, and related infections, supporting the development of stronger, more integrated health information systems. The guidelines also address the role of individual-level data in monitoring HIV prevention services, early diagnosis, late ART initiation, re-engagement in care, and advanced HIV disease. They highlight the integration of data on related infections (e.g., viral hepatitis, STIs, TB, and cervical cancer) to strengthen person-centered health services. Additionally, they emphasize the importance of governance, interoperability, data security, and privacy in transitioning from paper-based to digital systems. Digital health technologies are recognized as essential enablers of sustainable health systems and universal health coverage. To maximize their potential, digital health initiatives must address broader health information needs and be guided by robust strategies that integrate leadership, financial, organizational, human, and technological resources. These strategies should prioritize transparency, accessibility, scalability, interoperability, and data security. The guidelines were developed through a consultative process involving technical experts, health ministries, civil society, and development partners. They are organized into six technical chapters covering person-centered HIV prevention monitoring, patient monitoring, integration of related infections, routine data for surveillance, digital health data, and data use. The intended audience for these guidelines includes national and subnational HIV program managers, surveillance officers, and stakeholders involved in designing and using monitoring and evaluation systems. They are also relevant to technical partners, NGOs, private-sector care providers, and academic groups engaged in teaching and research. The guidelines aim to support countries in generating responsive, person-centered data to improve health decision-making and outcomes.
